segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: Dave, I’m worried about our case study. I’ve done a bit of reading, but I’m not sure what’s involved in actually writing a case study – I missed the lecture where Dr Baker talked us through it.

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: OK, well it’s quite straightforward. We’ve got our focus – that’s tourism at the Horton Castle site. And you said you’d done some reading about it.

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: Yes, I found some articles and made notes of the main points.

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: Did you remember to keep a record of where you got the information from? [[ ]]

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: Sure. I know what a pain it is when you forget that.

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: OK, so we can compare what we’ve read. Then we have to decide on a particular problem or need at our site. And then think about who we’re going to interview to get more information.

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: OK. So who’d that be? The people who work there [[ ]] ? And presumable some of the tourists too?

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: Yes, both those groups. So we’ll have to go to the site to do that, I suppose. But we might also do some of our interviewing away from the site – we could even contact some people here in the city, like administrators involved in overseeing tourism. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: OK. So we’ll need to think about our interview questions and fix times and places for the meetings. It’s all going to take a lot of time.

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: Mmm. And if we can, we should ask our interviewees if they can bring along some numerical data that we can add to support our findings.

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: And photographs?

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: I think we have plenty of those already. But Dr Baker also said we have to establish with our interviewees whether we can identify them in our case study, or whether they want to be anonymous. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: Oh, I wouldn’t have thought of that. OK, once we’ve got all this information, I suppose we have to analyse it.

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: Yes, put it all together and choose what’s relevant to the problem we’re focusing on, and analyse that carefully to find out if we can identify any trends or regularities [[ ]] there. That’s the main thing at this stage, rather can concentrating on details or lots of facts.

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: OK. And then once we’ve analysed that, what next?

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: Well, then we need to think about what we do with the data we’ve selected to make it as clear as possible to our readers. Things like graphs, or tables, or charts.

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: Right.

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: Then the case study itself is mostly quite standard; we begin by presenting the problem, and giving some background, then go through the main sections, but the thing that surprised me is that in a normal report we’d end with some suggestions to deal with the problem or need we identified, but in a case study we end up with a question or a series of questions to our readers, and they decide what ought to be done. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: Oh, I hadn’t realised that. ————————–

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: So basically, the problem we’re addressing in our case study of the Horton Castle site is why so few tourists are visiting it. And we’ll find out more from our interviews, but I did find one report on the internet that suggested that one reason might be because as far as transport goes, access is difficult.

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: I read that too, but that report was actually written ten years ago, when the road there was really bad, but that’s been improved now. And I think there’s plenty of fascinating stuff there for a really good day out, but you’d never realise it from the castle website – maybe that’s the problem. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: Yes, it’s really dry and boring.

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: I read somewhere a suggestion that what the castle needs is a visitor centre. So we could have a look for some information about that on the internet. What would we need to know?

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: Well, who’d use it for a start. It’s be good to know what categories the visitors fell into too, like school parties or retired people, but I think we’d have to talk to staff to get that information.

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: OK. And as we’re thinking of suggesting a visitor centre we’d also have to look at potential problems. I mean, obviously it wouldn’t be cheap to set up.

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: No, but it could be a really good investment. And as it’s on a historical site it’d need to get special planning permission, I expect. That might be hard. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: Right, especially as the only possible place for it would be at the entrance, and that’s right in front of the castle.

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: Mmm.

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: But it could be a good thing for the town of Horton. At present it’s a bit of a ghost town. Once they’ve left school and got any skills or qualifications, the young people all get out as fast as they can to get jobs in the city, and the only people left are children and those who’ve retired. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: NATALIE
segments.en: Right. Something else we could investigate would be the potential damage that tourists might cause to the castle site, I mean their environmental impact. At present the tourists can just wander round wherever they want, but if numbers increase, there might have to be some restrictions, like sticking to marked ways. And there’d need to be guides and wardens around to make sure these were enforced. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: DAVE
segments.en: Yes, we could look at that too. OK, well ...
